title: Brotherhood, favoritism and the moral side of Masonry
summary: They discuss helping a brother in the music business, church obligations and how Masonry teaches everyday morality.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Life philosophy: faith, karma and how to live

blocks.x: Well now, how does this -- in the
music business, do you think one brother helps another when he can?
Yeah, he sure does.
I mean -- I mean suppose for the sake of argument you were putting a band together, and there were two trombone players equally good, would you take the brother rather than the non --
If he was a brother that I know didn't adhere to the principles of doing what he's supposed to do --
Oh, you wouldn't.
I'd take the other man.
Right. But I mean assuming that he's -- I mean in a way if you had the opportunity to favor a member of your lodge who was a -- you would do it?
Yes.
Well, that's what you're supposed to do.
(Simultaneous remarks)
Well, actually, I mean it gives you something in your -- you know, my father always claimed that if you lived up to it, you really didn't have to go to church.
It's true, because (unintelligible) in order with when you take the solemn obligation, you have to be the old man above.
You sure did.

You had to be in with him. Otherwise, that's the finish of that. And if he don't go to church, even with all the houses that he belong to, blue house, red house, the consistory or the knights of templars or the Shrines, everyone have a divine service, and that's -- you got to go to church five times a year if you never go at all if you're going to be a -- you know --
Well, I mean, you know, I mean quite apart from the kind of ritual of it, the moral --
(Simultaneous remarks)
That's true.
In other words, I mean you -- you really -- you're sort of confirming the fact that you don't believe in cheating, robbing --
That's true.
-- lying -- I mean, you know—
(Simultaneous remarks)
It's a good thing.
It's a good thing.
That's right.
You know, actually, Stanley, when you --
It's not like a Rotary Club, where -- you know, I mean a Rotary Club is a backslapping thing,
try to benefit each other, but that's a business thing.
Well, you will find a devil in all organizations.
Oh, sure.

And consequently -- but when you -- after you realize -- you get into it, you find out it's everyday life. You find a lot of people never belong to anything but just as conscientious toward (unintelligible) to your fellow man, and then when he gets in, he find out the precepts where he's at home. He says, well, this I've been doing all my life. Now I understand what it means. So he's a good man.
